assessment.nobel_worthiness: A clear discovery in the sense I care about: the first detection of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies, followed by the evidence for TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic-plane neutrinos, opened a genuinely new observational window and tells us about cosmic-ray accelerators. It was a measurement driven by nature, not by an elegant idea.
assessment.attribution: The decisive roles are the conception and construction of IceCube (Halzen as the driving scientist, Karle and Spiering in leadership of construction and analysis). A fair three-person prize is conceivable, but I am relying on recollection of the roles and the large collaboration plus the AMANDA precursors make allocation delicate.
assessment.maturity: Mature: the diffuse flux has been confirmed by several analyses and independently by ANTARES/Baikal and KM3NeT hints; source identification is still partial but the discovery itself is secure and timely.
uncertainties: Exact leadership credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and others (e.g. earlier DUMAND/AMANDA pioneers) is unresolved.
Source associations beyond a few objects are still at modest significance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* are direct empirical evidence for black holes with shadows consistent with general relativity, and have the existential and communicable weight the committee likes. The VLBI technique at 1.3 mm is itself a major experimental achievement.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept, Doeleman led the EHT and the VLBI technical build-up, Zensus built the European VLBI/ mm-VLBI capability. A three-person prize is possible but the work is a collaboration of hundreds and credit could be disputed; I treat the supplied names as the workable set.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature: M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022) with polarization follow-ups and repeat observations; interpretation of the images (accretion-flow modelling) still evolving.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views the result as an observation that tests gravity or as imaging technology.
Allocation among Falcke, Doeleman, Zensus and other EHT leaders.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The detection of the baryon acoustic peak in the galaxy correlation function (SDSS and 2dFGRS) gave a robust standard ruler and is central to the evidence for dark energy, which interests me closely. It is a clean observational discovery with a calibrated physical origin in the early-universe plasma.
assessment.attribution: Eisenstein and collaborators (SDSS LRG) and Cole/Peacock for the 2dFGRS detection are the natural trio, but the two groups published near-simultaneously in 2005 and others (e.g. Percival, Hu) contributed. Credit is plausible but not tidy.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: replicated by BOSS, eBOSS, DESI and in the CMB; DESI dynamical dark-energy hints are intriguing but do not affect the BAO discovery itself.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior cosmology prizes (2006, 2011, 2019) may reduce novelty for the committee.
Credit between SDSS and 2dFGRS teams is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect (Kane-Mele) and its experimental observation in HgTe wells (Molenkamp, with Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang theory) founded the field of topological insulators, with lasting impact on condensed matter and materials. Theory was confirmed by experiment, which I value.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele for the Z2 classification and spin Hall prediction; Molenkamp for experimental confirmation. Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Hasan and others also contributed and are not in this entry, so the allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Mature: nearly two decades of independent confirmation in 2D and 3D materials, quantum anomalous Hall, and applications to materials physics.
uncertainties: Omission of Zhang/Bernevig/Hughes/Fu/Hasan from the supplied credit is an acknowledged fairness gap.
Practical impact is still largely conceptual.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock (magic wavelength concept by Katori, and its realization at fractional uncertainty of 1e-18 by Ye) is a precision-measurement achievement with applications to tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice idea; Ye led the realization and best-in-class performance. A two-person prize is clean, with Hall and Hansch already recognized in 2005 for frequency combs.
assessment.maturity: Mature technologically, with multiple groups agreeing at the 1e-18 level; the redefinition of the second is still in preparation, so the full impact is not yet realized.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier frequency-comb prize and possible competing credit to trapped-ion clock groups.
Whether the committee sees this as an instrument rather than a discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theoretical prediction of flat bands at magic angles followed by the 2018 discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened moire quantum matter, a large and rapidly growing field. It combines a clear prediction with a striking experimental confirmation.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald for the continuum-model prediction, Jarillo-Herrero for the experimental discovery; Cao and others carried out the experiments. Credit is relatively compact but the junior experimental co-authors are omitted.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature but still young: replicated by many groups, though mechanism of superconductivity is unsettled.
uncertainties: Slightly early; the field is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson at 125 GeV completed the Standard Model and is a landmark of nature confirming a theoretical prediction; the theory was recognized in 2013. A second prize is only warranted if the experimental achievement is credited separately.
assessment.attribution: The detectors are collaborations of thousands. Jenni and Della Negra are founding figures of ATLAS and CMS and Gianotti led ATLAS at the discovery; Virdee also could be chosen. The prize rules and the three-person limit make this contested, so I am uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature: couplings measured with growing precision, but the discovery was twelve years ago and the fairness of picking individuals is the central issue.
uncertainties: Collaboration credit and the three-person limit make an individual allocation hard.
The 2013 prize may be read as having already settled recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong coupling between superconducting qubits and microwave photons a practical architecture for quantum computing and is the basis of modern superconducting processors. The importance and originality are high.
assessment.attribution: Blais for the theory proposal, Wallraff and Schoelkopf for the first strong-coupling experiments in 2004. Also tied to Devoret/Martinis/Clarke work recognized in 2025, which complicates the situation.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a technique with independent confirmation across many labs; recognition could be premature or overlap with 2025.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
